subject: More perfect fits in CAR models

messages.author: aae8e9f66c6ae74f
messages.subject: More perfect fits in CAR models
parts:
So I've been trying to fit some very basic CAR models, to check I know exactly what is going on with everything and have spotted, as others before, that I'm getting a perfect fit with the gaussian family models. Advice in posts before seemed to suggest solving it using a shrinkage prior, which makes sense to me. But I'm really not getting anywhere. This is essentially a null model - only with intercept and spatial effect, and really shouldn't fit perfectly. What am I doing wrong?! I sort of this the solution to this might help me with my larger problem...

pd.analysis.null <- inla(log(med.pd) ~ 1 +
                         f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "adj.txt", 
                           hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", fixed = FALSE, param = c(.1,0.5)))),
                         family = "gaussian", control.compute = list(dic=TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                         control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", fixed = FALSE, param = c(0.1,0.5)))),
                         data = variables, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))

Thanks!

Colin

On Fri, 2017-07-07 at 08:47 -0700, Colin Beale wrote:

> pd.analysis.null <- inla(log(med.pd) ~ 1 +
>                          f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "adj.txt", 
>                            hyper = list(prec = list(prior =
> "pc.prec", fixed = FALSE, param = c(.1,0.5)))),
>                          family = "gaussian", control.compute =
> list(dic=TRUE, waic = TRUE),
>                          control.family = list(hyper = list(prec =
> list(prior = "pc.prec", fixed = FALSE, param = c(0.1,0.5)))),
>                          data = variables, control.predictor =
> list(compute = TRUE))
>

one thing at least, if you're using prior='pc.prec', then also add

f(ID, model="besag", scale.model=TRUE,....)


otherwise, you do not know the prec=1 means.


If you having counts, and using family="gaussian" as a gaussian-approx,
then do sqrt instead of log, so I would try with this one:



pd.analysis.null <- inla(sqrt(med.pd) ~ 1 +
f(ID, model = "besag", graph = "adj.txt",
scale.model=TRUE,
hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec",

param = c(.1,0.5)))),
                         family = "gaussian", control.compute =
list(dic=TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                         control.family = list(hyper = list(prec =
list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(0.1,0.5)))),

data = variables, 
control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))

--
Håvard Rue

is wrong the normal response is to get no smoothing at all. also maybe
try to plot the data on the 'spatial locations' to verify the same

Do you really not get perfect fits?

Thanks!
Colin

parts:
Both components have pc-priors that "pull" the component marginal variances parameters toward zero. I suspect they are simply competing about which one get to be zero, and the besag model wins out, due to the presence of dependence. It may be worth adjusting the prior parameters for each component up and down and see if at some point, the results shitft. (Note: no actual mathematics went into these thoughts...)

Finn

So I've tried all possible combinations of low (0.1), medium (0.5) and high (0.9) of each parameter in the pc-priors, alternating across the two sets, I've also tried with loggamma priors and the default priors and whatever I do, I end up with perfect prediction and essentially the same posteriors. This can't be right!

Using ggplot I can confirm that the spatial mapping is correct (code below), and I've redone the adjacency graph a few times too, to no avail.

library(ggplot2)
variables$z <- pd.analysis.null$summary.fitted$mean
 ggplot(variables, aes(x, y, colour = z)) + geom_point() + scale_colour_gradient(low = "red", high = "blue")
 ggplot(variables, aes(x, y, colour = sqrt(med.pd)) + geom_point() + scale_colour_gradient(low = "red", high = "blue")

The pattern is very smooth, but there is variability in it - I can't believe the null model is perfect...

C

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] More perfect fits in CAR models
parts:
As you'll see, I've still not made any real progress here. I'm really at a loss - the null model can't be perfect! I've checked the graphs, I've scaled dependent variables, I've tried a wide range of priors, and I essentialyl end up with the same model each time, which make a perfect prediction. If it weren't for the perfect prediction, I would have happily taken the model as accurate. But I want to compare between the null model and a couple of alternatives that make ecological sense to me and obviously if the null model is perfect I don' know how to do this (although the parameter estimates for ecological meaningful models are well estimated and don't overlap zero, the QAIC and other measures are, of course, worse...).

It's driving me mad, and I'd love to get this to work!

Thanks,
Colin

parts:
Fixing the Gaussian at the variance of the data does, of course, work and might be the optimal solution. Otherwise, the information was in other parts of the threat I may have got hidden - all the data required are in the original dataset:

Here's the map:

library(ggplot2)
variables$z <- pd.analysis.null$summary.fitted$mean
 ggplot(variables, aes(x, y, colour = z)) + geom_point() + scale_colour_gradient(low = "red", high = "blue")
 ggplot(variables, aes(x, y, colour = sqrt(med.pd)) + geom_point() + scale_colour_gradient(low = "red", high = "blue")

the graph was generated:

library(spdep)
neighs <- dnearneigh(as.matrix(variables[,c("x", "y")]), d1 = 0, d2 = 0.06)  
nb2INLA( "adj.txt", neighs)

Unfortunately Cambridge is a little too far at the moment (also trying to write a grant...), but thanks for the invite!

C
